title: Vectors in 2D and 3D
summary: A [[vector|vector]] has a size and a direction, so it can describe a movement such as “4 across and 3 up”. You write vectors with components or with $\boldsymbol{i}$, $\boldsymbol{j}$ and $\boldsymbol{k}$, then add, subtract and scale them. Their lengths give distances in 3D, and their algebra proves facts about shapes.

goals.text: Draw a [[vector|vector]] as an arrow, and tell a [[position-vector|position vector]] from a [[displacement-vector|displacement vector]].
Write vectors as column vectors or with the [[base-vectors|base vectors]] $\boldsymbol{i}$, $\boldsymbol{j}$, $\boldsymbol{k}$.
Add, subtract and scale vectors, using the [[zero-vector|zero vector]] $\boldsymbol{0}$ and $-\boldsymbol{v}$.
Find a [[vector-magnitude|magnitude]], a [[unit-vector|unit vector]], $\overrightarrow{AB} = \boldsymbol{b} - \boldsymbol{a}$ and the distance $AB$.

before.prompt: Find the distance between the points $(2, -1, 3)$ and $(-2, 1, 7)$.
before.hint: Subtract matching coordinates, square, add, then take the square root.

before.prompt: Find the midpoint of the points $(3, -5, 2)$ and $(-1, 1, 8)$.
before.hint: Add matching coordinates, then halve each total.

blocks.text: A mass of 5 kg is only a size: a [[scalar|scalar]]. “Walk 300 m” is not enough to follow. “Walk 300 m north-east” is, because it adds a direction.

blocks.statement: A vector is a quantity with both a magnitude (its size) and a direction.
blocks.plain: A vector tells you how far and which way.

blocks.text: You draw a [[vector|vector]] as a directed line segment: an arrow. Its length is the magnitude and its arrowhead gives the direction.
The arrow from A to B is written $\overrightarrow{AB}$. A single vector is printed in bold, such as $\boldsymbol{v}$. By hand, underline it: $\underline{v}$.

blocks.alt: Square grid numbered 0 to 10 across and 0 to 6 up. Arrow P Q goes from (1, 2) to (5, 5). Arrow R S goes from (6, 0) to (10, 3), the same length and direction as P Q. Arrow T U goes from (9, 6) to (6, 2).
blocks.caption: $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{RS}$ are equal vectors: both go 4 across and 3 up.

blocks.statement: Two vectors are equal when they have the same magnitude and direction, wherever you draw them.
blocks.why: A vector records the movement, not where it starts.

blocks.text: Count the movement on the grid to get the components. $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ goes 4 right and 3 up, so it is the column vector $\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}$. Moves left or down are negative.

blocks.question: Use the grid in the figure to write $\overrightarrow{TU}$ as a column vector.
steps: The tail T is at $(9, 6)$ and the arrowhead U is at $(6, 2)$.
Across: 9 to 6 is 3 left, so the first component is $-3$.
Up: 6 to 2 is 4 down, so the second component is $-4$.
Check: 3 left and 4 down from $(9, 6)$ lands on $(6, 2)$, which is U.

blocks.text: Now fix an origin O. The [[position-vector|position vector]] of a point A is $\overrightarrow{OA}$, written $\boldsymbol{a}$. Its components are the coordinates of A: if A is $(2, -1, 5)$, then $\boldsymbol{a} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
A position vector always starts at O. A vector between two points, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}$, is a [[displacement-vector|displacement vector]]: the move from A to B.

blocks.prompt: The point E has coordinates $(-3, 0, 4)$. Write its position vector $\boldsymbol{e}$ as a column vector.
blocks.hint: $\boldsymbol{e} = \overrightarrow{OE}$ starts at O. Its components are the coordinates of E.
blocks.explain: The components of $\overrightarrow{OE}$ are the coordinates of E, including the 0. $\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\-4\end{pmatrix}$ is $\overrightarrow{EO}$, which points back to O.

blocks.text: In 3D a vector has three components, along the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes. The [[base-vectors|base vectors]] are one-unit steps along each axis:
Any vector is a sum of steps along the axes, so exam questions write it in either of two ways:

The numbers $v_{1}$, $v_{2}$ and $v_{3}$ are the components. A missing base vector means a zero component. In 2D there is no $\boldsymbol{k}$: $\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix} = 4\boldsymbol{i} + 3\boldsymbol{j}$.

blocks.question: The point D has position vector $\boldsymbol{d} = 6\boldsymbol{i} - \boldsymbol{k}$. Write $\boldsymbol{d}$ as a column vector, and write down the coordinates of D.
steps: The $\boldsymbol{i}$ term is $6\boldsymbol{i}$, so the first component is 6.
There is no $\boldsymbol{j}$ term, so the second component is 0.
$-\boldsymbol{k}$ means $-1\boldsymbol{k}$, so the third component is $-1$.
The coordinates of D are the components of its position vector: $(6, 0, -1)$.

blocks.hint: Which base vector is missing? Its component is 0.
blocks.explain: There is no $\boldsymbol{i}$ term, so the first component is 0. It uses $\boldsymbol{k}$, so it is a 3D vector.

blocks.text: Walk along $\boldsymbol{u}$, then along $\boldsymbol{v}$. The single arrow from your start to your finish is the sum $\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{v}$. So put the tail of $\boldsymbol{v}$ on the head of $\boldsymbol{u}$, then join start to finish.

blocks.alt: Arrow u, then arrow v drawn from the head of u. The arrow from the start of u to the head of v is u plus v. Dashed copies of v then u, taken in the other order, complete a parallelogram and end at the same point.
blocks.caption: Taking $\boldsymbol{v}$ first, then $\boldsymbol{u}$, reaches the same point, so $\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{u}$.

blocks.text: With components, add matching components: moves along the same axis add up.
The [[zero-vector|zero vector]] $\boldsymbol{0}$ has every component 0. It is the move that goes nowhere, so $\boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{0} = \boldsymbol{v}$.

The [[vector|vector]] $-\boldsymbol{v}$ has the same length as $\boldsymbol{v}$ but points the opposite way. So $\boldsymbol{v} + (-\boldsymbol{v}) = \boldsymbol{0}$, and $\overrightarrow{BA} = -\overrightarrow{AB}$ for any two points.
Subtracting means adding the negative: $\boldsymbol{u} - \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{u} + (-\boldsymbol{v})$. With components, subtract matching components.

blocks.question: Given $\boldsymbol{u} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}$, $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{w} = 2\boldsymbol{j} - 6\boldsymbol{k}$, find $\boldsymbol{u} - \boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{w}$.
steps: Write $\boldsymbol{w}$ as a column vector. It has no $\boldsymbol{i}$ term, so $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-6\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.text: To get from A to B, you can go back from A to O, then out from O to B:

blocks.alt: Origin O with arrows to points A and B, labelled a and b. A third arrow goes from A to B and is labelled b minus a.

blocks.text: Read it as “end minus start”.
Writing $\overrightarrow{AB} = \boldsymbol{a} - \boldsymbol{b}$. That is $\overrightarrow{BA}$, the same arrow pointing backwards. Take the end point minus the start point.

blocks.question: The points A and B have coordinates $(4, -1, 2)$ and $(1, 3, -5)$. Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
steps: Check: A plus $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is $(4 - 3, -1 + 4, 2 - 7) = (1, 3, -5)$, which is B.

blocks.prompt: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-6\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and A is the point $(-1, 4, 3)$. Find the coordinates of B.

blocks.text: Without numbers, write the arrow you need as a route made of arrows you know.

blocks.prompt: PQRS is a parallelogram with $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \boldsymbol{u}$ and $\overrightarrow{PS} = \boldsymbol{w}$. Find $\overrightarrow{QS}$ in terms of $\boldsymbol{u}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$.
blocks.hint: Go from Q back to P, then from P to S.
blocks.explain: $\overrightarrow{QS} = \overrightarrow{QP} + \overrightarrow{PS} = -\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{w}$: end minus start, measured from P.

blocks.text: $\boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{v}$ is two copies of $\boldsymbol{v}$ end to end. It points the same way and is twice as long, so you write it $2\boldsymbol{v}$.
For any [[scalar|scalar]] $k$, multiply every component by $k$. If $k > 0$, $k\boldsymbol{v}$ points the same way as $\boldsymbol{v}$; if $k < 0$, the opposite way.

blocks.question: Given $\boldsymbol{a} = 2\boldsymbol{i} - 3\boldsymbol{j} + \boldsymbol{k}$ and $\boldsymbol{b} = -\boldsymbol{i} + 4\boldsymbol{j}$, find $3\boldsymbol{a} - 2\boldsymbol{b}$.
steps: Write both as column [[vector|vectors]]: $\boldsymbol{a} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{b} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\0\end{pmatrix}$. There is no $\boldsymbol{k}$ in $\boldsymbol{b}$.

blocks.statement: Two non-zero vectors $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ are parallel when $\boldsymbol{w} = k\boldsymbol{v}$ for some scalar $k$.
blocks.plain: One is a stretched, shrunk or reversed copy of the other.

blocks.text: To test whether two vectors are [[parallel-vectors|parallel]], divide matching components. If every ratio is the same number $k$, they are parallel. A zero component must match a zero component.

blocks.question: The vectors $\begin{pmatrix}6\\s\\-9\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\t\end{pmatrix}$ are parallel. Find the value of $s$ and the value of $t$.
steps: Parallel means $\begin{pmatrix}6\\s\\-9\end{pmatrix} = k\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\t\end{pmatrix}$, so $6 = -4k$, $s = 2k$ and $-9 = kt$.

blocks.hint: Look for one number $k$ that multiplies all three components.
blocks.explain: $\begin{pmatrix}-6\\12\\-4\end{pmatrix} = -2\begin{pmatrix}3\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}$. It points the opposite way, but it is still parallel.

blocks.text: Three points are [[collinear|collinear]] when one straight line passes through all of them. Parallel arrows can lie on different lines, so use two arrows that share a point.

blocks.statement: A, B and C are collinear when $\overrightarrow{AC} = k\overrightarrow{AB}$ for some scalar $k$.
blocks.why: Both arrows are parallel and start at A, so they lie on one line through A.

blocks.question: The points $A(2, -1, 3)$, $B(5, 1, 2)$ and $C(11, t, 0)$ are collinear. Find the value of $t$.
steps: Collinear means $\overrightarrow{AC} = k\overrightarrow{AB}$. The first components give $9 = 3k$, so $k = 3$. The third components agree: $-3 = 3 \times (-1)$.
The second components must match too: $t + 1 = 3 \times 2 = 6$, so $t = 5$.
So $\overrightarrow{AC} = 3\overrightarrow{AB}$: C is three times as far from A as B is.

blocks.prompt: The points $P(1, 4)$, $Q(3, 1)$ and $R(k, -8)$ are collinear. Find $k$.
blocks.hint: Compare the second components of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}$ to find the scalar.

blocks.text: The [[vector-magnitude|magnitude]] $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$ of a [[vector|vector]] is the length of its arrow. In 2D the components are the short sides of a right-angled triangle, so $\left\lvert\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert = \sqrt{4^{2} + 3^{2}} = 5$.
In 3D, use Pythagoras twice, as for a cuboid's space diagonal in {{lesson:3.1}}. The formula is in the booklet:

In 2D, leave out $v_{3}$. A magnitude is a [[scalar|scalar]] and is never negative. Also $\lvert -\boldsymbol{v}\rvert = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$, and $\lvert k\boldsymbol{v}\rvert = \lvert k\rvert\,\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$.

blocks.statement: A unit vector has magnitude 1. The unit vector in the direction of a non-zero vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ is $\frac{\boldsymbol{v}}{\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert}$.

blocks.text: So divide every component by $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$. The [[base-vectors|base vectors]] $\boldsymbol{i}$, $\boldsymbol{j}$ and $\boldsymbol{k}$ are [[unit-vector|unit vectors]]. For length $L$ in the direction of $\boldsymbol{v}$, use $L\frac{\boldsymbol{v}}{\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert}$; for the opposite direction, use $-L$.

blocks.question: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\boldsymbol{v} = 4\boldsymbol{i} - 4\boldsymbol{j} + 7\boldsymbol{k}$.

blocks.prompt: Find the vector of magnitude 12 in the opposite direction to $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
blocks.hint: Find its magnitude first. Opposite means a negative scalar.
blocks.explain: The magnitude is $\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$. So the answer is $-\frac{12}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix} = -4\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-8\\4\\-8\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.text: The distance between two points is the length of the arrow that joins them:
It is the distance formula from {{lesson:3.1}}, written with vectors.

blocks.question: The points A and B have [[position-vector|position vectors]] $\boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{i} - 2\boldsymbol{j}$ and $\boldsymbol{b} = 4\boldsymbol{i} + 2\boldsymbol{j} - 5\boldsymbol{k}$. Find the exact distance $AB$.
steps: Write $\boldsymbol{a}$ as a 3D column vector. There is no $\boldsymbol{k}$, so $\boldsymbol{a} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}$.
Simplify the surd: $\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25}\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}$. On Paper 1, leave it exact.

blocks.question: The point P is $(2, -1, 3)$ and the point Q is $(t, 2t, 1 - t)$, where $t$ is a real number. Use your calculator to find the values of $t$ for which $PQ = 7$. Give your answers to 3 s.f.
steps: Rearrange to $6t^{2} + 4t - 40 = 0$. Write this down before using your calculator: it earns the method mark.
The root finder gives $t = -2.9367\ldots$ and $t = 2.2700\ldots$. Both are valid.

ti84: Choose Poly Root Finder, set the degree to 2 (check on your model)
Enter the coefficients 6, 4 and -40, then SOLVE (check on your model)
nspire: Calculator page, Menu, Algebra, Polynomial Tools
Find Roots of Polynomial, degree 2, real roots (check on your model)
casio: Enter a = 6, b = 4 and c = -40, then SOLVE (check on your model)

blocks.text: When a length is given, square it first. Working with $PQ^{2} = 49$ keeps square roots out of the algebra.

blocks.prompt: Given $\boldsymbol{u} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$, find $\lvert 2\boldsymbol{u} - \boldsymbol{v}\rvert$. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Find the vector $2\boldsymbol{u} - \boldsymbol{v}$ first, then its magnitude.

blocks.text: [[vector|Vectors]] turn a geometry problem into algebra. Write every arrow in terms of a few vectors you know, then read the geometry off the algebra.
1. Choose two vectors to build from that are not [[parallel-vectors|parallel]], such as the [[position-vector|position vectors]] $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$.
2. Write each vector you need as a route, such as $\overrightarrow{AB} = \boldsymbol{b} - \boldsymbol{a}$.
3. Read off the geometry. A [[scalar|scalar]] multiple $k$ means parallel, with lengths in the ratio $\lvert k\rvert$. Equal position vectors mean the same point.

blocks.statement: The midpoint M of [AB] has position vector $\boldsymbol{m} = \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{a} + \boldsymbol{b})$.

blocks.text: This is the midpoint formula from {{lesson:3.1}}, written with vectors.

blocks.alt: Triangle O A B with arrow a from O to A and arrow b from O to B. M is the midpoint of O A and N is the midpoint of O B. A dashed arrow joins M to N, parallel to A B.

blocks.question: In triangle OAB, $\overrightarrow{OA} = \boldsymbol{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \boldsymbol{b}$. M is the midpoint of [OA] and N is the midpoint of [OB]. Find $\overrightarrow{MN}$ in terms of $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$. Hence show that [MN] is parallel to [AB] and half its length.
steps: M is halfway along [OA], so $\overrightarrow{OM} = \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{a}$. Likewise $\overrightarrow{ON} = \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{b}$.
Conclude in words: $\overrightarrow{MN}$ is a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, so [MN] is parallel to [AB], and it is half as long.

blocks.question: ABCD is a parallelogram with $\overrightarrow{AB} = \boldsymbol{u}$ and $\overrightarrow{AD} = \boldsymbol{w}$. X is the midpoint of the diagonal [BD]. Find $\overrightarrow{AX}$ in terms of $\boldsymbol{u}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$. Hence prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
steps: Opposite sides are equal vectors, so $\overrightarrow{BC} = \boldsymbol{w}$ and the diagonal $\overrightarrow{AC} = \boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{w}$.
Route to X: A to B, then halfway along [BD]. $\overrightarrow{AX} = \boldsymbol{u} + \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{u} + \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{w}$.
So $\overrightarrow{AX} = \frac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AC}$: X is also the midpoint of [AC]. The diagonals share a midpoint, so they bisect each other.

blocks.prompt: In triangle OAB, $\overrightarrow{OA} = \boldsymbol{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \boldsymbol{b}$. M is the midpoint of [AB], and G is the point on [OM] with $\overrightarrow{OG} = \frac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{OM}$. Find $\overrightarrow{OG}$.
blocks.hint: Find $\overrightarrow{OM}$ with the midpoint result first.

blocks.prompt: $\overrightarrow{OA} = \boldsymbol{a}$, $\overrightarrow{OB} = \boldsymbol{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{OC} = 3\boldsymbol{b} - 2\boldsymbol{a}$, where $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$ are not parallel. Which statement is true?
blocks.hint: Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ with end minus start, then compare them.

options.text: C is not on the line (AB)

blocks.explain: $\overrightarrow{AC} = (3\boldsymbol{b} - 2\boldsymbol{a}) - \boldsymbol{a} = 3\boldsymbol{b} - 3\boldsymbol{a} = 3(\boldsymbol{b} - \boldsymbol{a}) = 3\overrightarrow{AB}$. The arrows are parallel and share A, so A, B and C are [[collinear|collinear]].

blocks.text: The scalar product in {{lesson:3.13}} adds a test for right angles.
$\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}v_{1}\\v_{2}\\v_{3}\end{pmatrix} = v_{1}\boldsymbol{i} + v_{2}\boldsymbol{j} + v_{3}\boldsymbol{k}$. A missing base vector means a zero component.
$\overrightarrow{AB} = \boldsymbol{b} - \boldsymbol{a}$ (end minus start), and the distance $AB = \lvert\boldsymbol{b} - \boldsymbol{a}\rvert$.
Non-zero $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ are parallel when $\boldsymbol{w} = k\boldsymbol{v}$. A, B and C are collinear when $\overrightarrow{AC} = k\overrightarrow{AB}$.
Unit vector in the direction of $\boldsymbol{v}$: $\frac{\boldsymbol{v}}{\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert}$. Length $L$ in that direction: $L\frac{\boldsymbol{v}}{\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert}$.
The midpoint of [AB] has position vector $\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{a} + \boldsymbol{b})$.
Vector proof: write every arrow in terms of two non-parallel vectors such as $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$. A scalar multiple means parallel; equal position vectors mean the same point.

mistakes: Losing a sign when subtracting a negative component: $3 - (-2) = 5$, not $1$. Bracket negative components first.
Writing $-4^{2}$ for a component of $-4$ in a magnitude. That is $-16$; you need $(-4)^{2} = 16$.
Dividing only some components to make a unit vector. Divide every component by $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$.
Calling points collinear because two arrows are parallel, with no shared point. Use arrows that both start at the same point.
Giving a point when the question asks for a vector, or a vector when it asks for a distance. Re-read the question first.
examTips: In a **show that** or **prove** question, write each route you use. End with a sentence that gives the reason, such as “a scalar multiple, so parallel”. A bare conclusion loses the reasoning mark.
On Paper 1, give magnitudes exact, as a surd such as $5\sqrt{2}$ (simplified is neater), not the decimal $7.07$.
On Paper 2, write down the equation you put into your calculator, then give each answer to 3 s.f.
